1.problem: Does there exist a prime \(p\) and distinct positive integers \(y_1, y_2, y_3\) with \(y_i < \frac{p}{3}\) for each \(1 \le i \le 3\) and \(y_1^3 \equiv y_2^3 \equiv y_3^3 \pmod{p}\)?
1.solutions:
Note that \(y_1, y_2, y_3 ot\equiv 0 \pmod{p}\). So if \(y_1^3 \equiv y_2^3 \equiv y_3^3\), then \(\left( rac{y_2}{y_1} ight)^3 \equiv \left( rac{y_3}{y_1} ight)^3 \equiv 1 \pmod{p}\).

Thus, \(y_2 y_1^{-1}\) and \(y_3 y_1^{-1}\) are distinct nonzero cube roots of \(1\) in \(\pmod{p}\).

We claim that if \(p \equiv 1 \pmod{3}\) then there are exactly three cube roots of \(1\) \(\pmod{p}\), and they are \(1, \alpha, \alpha^2\) for some residue \(\alpha\), and if \(p ot\equiv 1 \pmod{3}\) then the only cube root of \(1\) \(\pmod{p}\) is \(1\). This is because of primitive roots; if \(g\) is a primitive root \(\pmod{p}\) and \(p e 3\) then \(g^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{3}\), so if \(p \equiv 1 \pmod{3}\) then the cube roots of \(1\) are \(1, g^{ rac{p-1}{3}}, g^{2 \cdot rac{p-1}{3}}\), and if \(p ot\equiv 1 \pmod{3}\) then the only cube root of \(1\) in \(\pmod{p}\) is \(1\).

Thus, assuming that \(p \equiv 1 \pmod{3}\), we must have \(\{y_2 y_1^{-1}, y_3 y_1^{-1}\} = \{\alpha, \alpha^2\}\). So, \[y_1 + y_2 + y_3 = y_1(1 + \alpha + \alpha^2) = y_1 \left( rac{\alpha^3 - 1}{\alpha - 1} ight).\]

\(\alpha e 1\) and \(\alpha^3 = 1\) since \(\alpha\) is a cube root of unity in \(\pmod{p}\), so \(y_1 + y_2 + y_3 \equiv 0 \pmod{p}\). If \(0 < y_1, y_2, y_3 < rac{p}{3}\), then \(0 < y_1 + y_2 + y_3 < p\), so it is impossible for \(y_1 + y_2 + y_3 \equiv 0 \pmod{p}\). Thus, the answer is no.

2.problem: The \(n\) vertices of a regular \(n\)-gon are drawn, and each of the \(\binom{n}{2}\) edges between them is colored such that no two edges of the same color intersect at a point which is not a vertex of the \(n\)-gon. What is the minimum number of different colors that can be used to color all the edges?
2.solutions:
The answer is \(\lceil \frac{n}{2} \rceil\). First we will show that we need \(\ge \lceil \frac{n}{2} \rceil\) colors. For \(n\) even, consider the \(\frac{n}{2}\) longest diagonals (that go through the center of the \(n\)-gon); all of these intersect each other so they must be different colors. For \(n\) odd, consider the \(n\) longest diagonals, which form a star. Let two of these diagonals be called ”adjacent” if they are adjacent edges of the star, AKA they share a vertex of the \(n\)-gon. Then all non-adjacent pairs of diagonals among these \(n\) longest diagonals intersect each other, so if two of them are the same color then they must be adjacent. This implies that we need \(\ge \lceil \frac{n}{2} \rceil\) colors.

Now for the construction; we will show that \(\lceil \frac{n}{2} \rceil\) colors is enough. Consider the following zigzag sequences of \(n-1\) edges, drawn in red, for the \(n = 8\) and \(n = 7\) cases.

For \(n\) even, we can overlay \(\frac{n}{2}\) of them (the original, its rotation by \(\frac{360^\circ}{n}\), its rotation by \(2 \cdot \frac{360^\circ}{n}\), …, its rotation by \(\left(\frac{n}{2}-1\right)\frac{360^\circ}{n}\)), and have each copy be a different color. For \(n\) odd, we can overlay \(\frac{n-1}{2}\) of these zigzag paths (rotation by \(0^\circ\) through rotation by \(\left(\frac{n-3}{2}\right)\frac{360^\circ}{n}\)) in the same way as for the \(n\) even case, and then the last \(\frac{n-1}{2}\) edges, which make up half of a ”copy” themselves, will be colored with the \(\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)\)th color.

So, it is possible to use just \(\lceil \frac{n}{2} \rceil\) colors, but we also must use at least this many, and so \(\boxed{\lceil \frac{n}{2} \rceil}\) is the answer.

5.problem:
Let \(\mathbb{Q}\) denote the set of rational numbers. Suppose \(f : \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{Q}\) is a function that satisfies \(0 < |f(x) - f(y)| \le |x - y|\) for all \(x \ne y \in \mathbb{Q}\). Must \(f\) be monotonic?

A function \(f\) is increasing if \(f(x) < f(y)\) whenever \(x < y\). A function \(f\) is monotonic if either \(f\) or \(-f\) is increasing.
5.solutions: The answer is no. Consider the function \[f(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{1+x}\right)^2 & \text{if } x > 3 - 2\sqrt{2} \\ \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{1}{1-x}\right)^2 & \text{if } x < 3 - 2\sqrt{2} \end{cases}\] with its domain extended to all real numbers. Clearly, \(f(x)\) is rational for any rational \(x\). Now we shall show that for any real numbers \(x\) and \(y\), we have \(|f(x) - f(y)| \le |x-y|\). We first show that this holds in the case where \(y > x \ge 3 - 2\sqrt{2}\). Note that \[f(x) - f(y) = \frac{1}{2}\left(\left(\frac{1}{1+x}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{1}{1+y}\right)^2\right) = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{1+x} + \frac{1}{1+y}\right)\left(\frac{1}{1+x} - \frac{1}{1+y}\right)\] Since \(\frac{1}{1+y} < \frac{1}{1+x} \le \frac{2+\sqrt{2}}{4}\), it follows that \[f(x) - f(y) = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{1+x} + \frac{1}{1+y}\right)\left(\frac{y-x}{(1+x)(1+y)}\right) \le \left(\frac{2+\sqrt{2}}{4}\right)^3 (y-x) < y - x\] Now we consider the case where \(x < y \le 3 - 2\sqrt{2}\). As before, note that \[f(y) - f(x) = \frac{1}{4}\left(\left(\frac{1}{1-y}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{1}{1-x}\right)^2\right) = \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{1}{1-x} + \frac{1}{1-y}\right)\left(\frac{1}{1-y} - \frac{1}{1-x}\right)\] Since \(\frac{1}{1-x} < \frac{1}{1-y} \le \frac{1+\sqrt{2}}{2}\), it follows that \[f(x) - f(y) = \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{1}{1-x} + \frac{1}{1-y}\right)\left(\frac{y-x}{(1-x)(1-y)}\right) \le \frac{1}{2} \cdot \left(\frac{1+\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)^3 (y-x) < y - x\] In the case where \(x \le 3 - 2\sqrt{2} \le y\), we have that \[\begin{aligned} |f(x) - f(y)| &\le |f(x) - f(3-2\sqrt{2})| + |f(3-2\sqrt{2}) - f(y)| \\ &\le |x - (3-2\sqrt{2})| + |(3-2\sqrt{2}) - y| \\ &= |x-y| \end{aligned}\] Lastly, it remains to show that for any rational numbers \(r \ne s\), we have \(f(r) \ne f(s)\). Indeed, \(f(x)\) is increasing for \(x < 3-2\sqrt{2}\) and decreasing for \(x > 3-2\sqrt{2}\), so \(f(r) \ne f(s)\) if both \(r\) and \(s\) are less than \(3-2\sqrt{2}\), or both are greater than \(3-2\sqrt{2}\). On the other hand, if WLOG \(r < 3-2\sqrt{2} < s\), then \[\frac{f(r)}{f(s)} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1+s}{1-r}\right)^2 \ne 1\] since \(2\) is not the square of a rational number. This completes the proof.

7.problem: Puddles the Frog has a row of \(n \ge 2\) lilypads, labeled \(1\) through \(n\), with \(1\) unit between consecutive lilypads. He is at lilypad \(1\), and wishes to visit lilypads \(2\) through \(n\) once each, before ending up back at lilypad \(1\). However, he may jump no more than \(3\) units at a time. Let \(f(n)\) be the maximum total distance of Puddles’s trip, starting from lilypad \(1\) and ending back at lilypad \(1\). Determine, with proof, the value of \[\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{f(n)}{n}.\]
7.solutions:
The answer is \(\boxed{\frac{14}{5}}\). Consider each of the \(2024\) unit segments between consecutive lilypads. Each segment must be covered an even number of times and at least twice.

Here is a construction for \(\approx \frac{2}{5}\) of the segments to be covered \(4\) times and the rest to be covered \(2\) times. It uses \(20\) lilypads, but can be extended to infinitely large numbers by inserting more sections of \(5\) unit segments (covered \(4,4,2,2,2\) times) in the middle. The numbers underneath the unit segments are the number of times each segment is covered.

Claim 1: It is impossible for any segment to be covered more than \(4\) times.

Let \(F, E, D, A, B, C\) be \(6\) consecutive lilypads in that order. We will be analyzing the segment between \(A\) and \(D\), which we will call \(AD\). Because each jump is at most \(3\) units in length, each jump that goes over \(AD\) must be between one of \(\{A,B,C\}\) and one of \(\{D,E,F\}\). Since each node in this graph has degree \(2\), there are at most \(6\) such jumps, but \(F\) and \(C\) can each only be used once (because we can’t repeat any one jump), so there are at most \(5\) jumps. Since each segment must be covered an even number of times, \(AD\) must be covered at most \(4\) times.

Claim 2: Each occurrence of \(4\) must either be surrounded by three \(2\)’s on either side, like \(2\ 2\ 2\ 4\ 2\ 2\ 2\), or adjacent to another \(4\) and together they are surrounded by three \(2\)’s on either side, like \(2\ 2\ 2\ 4\ 2\ 2\ 2\) (unless they get cut off by the row ending, in which case some of the \(2\)’s can get cut off).

Suppose \(AD\) is covered \(4\) times. The \(4\) jumps that cover \(AD\) must have one endpoint in \(\{A,B,C\}\) and one endpoint in \(\{D,E,F\}\). Thus, by pigeonhole, at least one of \(\{A,B,C\}\) must be the endpoint of two jumps that cover \(AD\). It cannot be \(C\), so it must be either \(A\) or \(B\) or both. If it is both, then all \(4\) jumps that cover \(AD\) have \(A\) or \(B\) as their right endpoint, which is bad because it means Puddles does not visit \(C\) nor anything to the right of \(C\). This is okay if and only if \(B\) is the very last lilypad (so lilypad \(C\) does not even exist). And we can see that in this case, \(AB\) is covered twice.

Normally, (if \(C\) exists) exactly one of \(\{A,B\}\) would be the endpoint of two jumps that cover \(AD\). Let this vertex be called the ”bounce vertex”. Then we have two different cases: \(A\) is the ”bounce vertex”, or \(B\) is the ”bounce vertex”. Similarly, there is one ”bounce vertex” on the left side, and it is either \(D\) or \(E\). Through experimentation, we find that if A, B, C, D, E, F all exist, then if \(B\) is the ”bounce vertex” on the right, \(D\) must be the ”bounce vertex” on the left.

This causes \(AD\) to be covered \(4\) times, \(AB\) to be covered \(4\) times, and each of the three segments to the left of \(AD\) and each of the three segments to the right of \(AB\) to all be covered \(2\) times, since in order for a segment to be covered \(4\) times, it must have a ”bounce vertex” among the \(3\) lilypads to its left, and a ”bounce vertex” among the \(3\) lilypads to its right.

Similarly, if \(E\) is the ”bounce vertex” on the left, then \(A\) must be the ”bounce vertex” on the right, and the diagram looks like the flipped version of this.

The last case that we must consider is where \(A\) and \(D\) are the two ”bounce vertices”, and then through experimentation we have these two cases:

However, the first one is actually impossible because the path would be two disjoint loops in this case. In the second case, \(AD\) is covered \(4\) times and the three segments to the left of \(AD\) and the three segments to the right of \(AD\) each must be covered only twice.

Thus, Claim 2 is proven, and the construction at the beginning of the solution (which can be extended for larger numbers of lilypads) shows that it’s possible for \(\approx \frac{2}{5}\) of the segments to be covered \(4\) times, and the other \(\approx \frac{3}{5}\) to be covered \(2\) times, yielding an answer of \(\frac{4+4+2+2+2}{5} = \boxed{\frac{14}{5}}\).
